about: Writing tasks for testing the write-like-myself skill. Each task gives an agent everything it needs to know, so that a rejected text reflects the writing and not missing facts. The prompt is worded the way Yili types. Facts and materials go to the agent as notes.md and named files; expectations are checked afterwards and are never shown to the agent. Tasks on unpublished work are kept in the private folder.

tasks.prompt: write the abstract for the dataset paper, 200 words max
tasks.audience: Readers of a data journal: Earth scientists and machine-learning researchers who work on permafrost.
facts: Retrogressive thaw slumps (RTS) form when ice-rich permafrost on a slope thaws abruptly; they reshape Arctic hillslopes and can release carbon.
Where RTS occur across the Arctic is poorly known, because mapping them by hand is slow and has been done one region at a time.
Many research groups have published their own RTS digitisations, but in different formats and with no shared standard, which limits large studies and the training of deep learning models.
We combined 20 of these separate datasets into one, called ARTS (Arctic Retrogressive Thaw Slumps).
ARTS holds 23,529 digitisations where an RTS is present and 20,434 where none is present.
We also propose a data curation framework: guidelines for digitising, a metadata format, an indexing scheme, a storage format and rules for contributing.
The dataset is open, its changes are tracked with Git, and it is hosted on GitHub and at the Arctic Data Center. We expect new contributions.
expectations: Opens with the phenomenon or the problem, not with 'In this paper' or 'This study'
Every number appears in the facts
States what the dataset contains and what it makes possible
Claims no primacy or superlative that the facts do not give

tasks.prompt: write the results paragraph for this table. just the results, the discussion comes later
tasks.audience: Readers of a remote sensing journal.
facts: The table in results_table.md is the full set of results for this paragraph.
The model is a U-Net with an EfficientNet-B3 encoder.
Test tiles were held out by region. Banks Island tiles were never used in training.

materials.results_table.md:
| Training regions | Test region | IoU | Precision | Recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yamal only | Yamal | 0.74 | 0.81 | 0.79 |
| Yamal only | Banks Island | 0.41 | 0.66 | 0.48 |
| Yamal and five other regions | Yamal | 0.73 | 0.80 | 0.79 |
| Yamal and five other regions | Banks Island | 0.62 | 0.74 | 0.71 |

IoU is intersection over union on held-out test tiles.

expectations: Reports the fall from 0.74 to 0.41 IoU when the Yamal-only model is tested on Banks Island
Reports the rise to 0.62 on Banks Island with multi-region training, and that Yamal stays about the same
Gives no explanation of why (interpretation belongs to the Discussion)
The first sentence states the main finding

tasks.prompt: turn my notes into the methods paragraph on how we split the data
tasks.audience: Journal readers who may want to repeat the work.
facts: Image tiles are 512 by 512 pixels of PlanetScope imagery at 3 m.
Tiles were split by ecoregion, not tile by tile, so that neighbouring tiles never end up in both training and test data.
There are 14 ecoregions: 10 for training, 2 for validation and 2 for testing.
The validation set was used to choose the detection threshold and to stop training. The test set was scored once, at the end.
Background tiles were sampled so that RTS tiles make up 1 in 200 tiles in the validation and test sets, about the rate the model meets when mapping.
The training set has more RTS tiles (1 in 10) so that the model sees enough examples.
expectations: States that the split is by ecoregion and why (neighbouring tiles would leak between sets)
States the 1-in-200 rate for validation and test and the 1-in-10 rate for training, with the reason for each
States that the test set was scored once

tasks.prompt: draft a discussion paragraph on why adding other regions helped on banks island. careful not to overclaim, we didn't test the reasons directly
tasks.audience: Readers of a remote sensing journal.
facts: Result: a model trained on Yamal only reached IoU 0.41 on Banks Island; trained on Yamal and five other regions it reached 0.62. On Yamal itself both reached about 0.74.
Possible reason 1: slumps on Banks Island are larger and form in different surface materials from those on Yamal.
Possible reason 2: the multi-region model saw a wider range of headwall shapes and vegetation backgrounds.
Observation: most of the Yamal-only model's missed slumps on Banks Island had bright, unvegetated floors, which are rare on Yamal and common on Banks Island.
We ran no experiment that isolates any single reason.
Earlier regional studies reported similar losses when models were moved to new regions. No specific citation is available yet; leave a placeholder.
expectations: Keeps the result and the explanations apart, and marks the explanations as untested
Uses the observation about bright floors as evidence, not as proof
Invents no citation (a placeholder is fine)
Ends on what the finding means for choosing training data

tasks.prompt: caption for figure 3. keep it short
tasks.audience: Journal readers looking at the figure.
facts: Figure 3 has four panels.
(a) PlanetScope image of a slump on the Yamal Peninsula, July 2023.
(b) The manual label of that slump.
(c) The model's probability map for the same tile, from 0 to 1.
(d) The detection after a 0.5 threshold, drawn over the image: true positive in green, false positive in red.
Each panel has a 500 m scale bar. The legend already shows the colour scale.
expectations: Opens with a brief summary of the figure, then gives each panel its own short sentence
Does not repeat what the legend shows

tasks.prompt: write 4 highlights for the SAM paper, each under 85 characters including spaces
tasks.audience: Journal readers scanning the article page.
facts: Maps of features in fast-changing landscapes, such as thawing permafrost, go out of date quickly.
We used old, outdated outlines as location prompts for the Segment Anything Model (SAM), which then segments the features in current satellite images without task-specific training.
The framework has two parts: an automated pipeline that prompts SAM with the historical outlines, and an interactive tool in which experts correct the results.
Case study: retrogressive thaw slumps.
Best intersection over union for routine updates: 0.80 plus or minus 0.10.
Quality matched manual digitising by experts, in half the time.
The framework does not depend on a particular model or task.
expectations: Each bullet is at most 85 characters including spaces
Each bullet states a finding or contribution plainly

tasks.prompt: make this easier to read. don't change the meaning
tasks.audience: Readers of a remote sensing journal.
facts: The paragraph to edit is in paragraph.md.
Every factual claim in it is correct and must stay.

materials.paragraph.md: Wildfires in the Arctic-boreal zone — a region warming roughly four times faster than the global average — are reshaping the carbon balance of northern ecosystems; yet our ability to quantify their footprint remains fundamentally constrained by the patchwork of existing burned-area products, which, despite decades of methodological refinement, continue to disagree markedly in both extent and timing. Crucially, this disagreement is not merely a technical nuisance: it propagates directly into carbon emission estimates, creating a cascade of uncertainty that undermines efforts to close the northern carbon budget. Here, we leverage the synergistic potential of Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery to deliver a robust, harmonised burned-area record that bridges this critical gap.

expectations: Keeps every claim: the warming rate, the disagreement between products in extent and timing, its effect on carbon emission estimates, and the combined Landsat and Sentinel-2 record
The dash aside, the semicolon and the colon explanation are gone or rewritten as plain sentences
Words that only add importance (crucially, synergistic, robust, critical gap, leverage) are gone
Sentences are shorter and still linked

tasks.prompt: this results paragraph has discussion mixed in. fix it, keep only results here and give me the interpretation bits separately
tasks.audience: Readers of a remote sensing journal.
facts: The paragraph is in paragraph.md.
Return the results paragraph, then, under a separate heading, the interpretations to move to the Discussion.

materials.paragraph.md: The model detected 18,412 water bodies smaller than 1 ha across the study area, 64% more than the existing inventory, which suggests that previous products have systematically overlooked the smallest ponds, most likely because their coarser resolution blurs pond edges into the surrounding tundra. Seasonal variability was pronounced: 31% of ponds present in June had disappeared by late August, a pattern we attribute to evaporation and drainage through thawing permafrost, highlighting the vulnerability of these systems to continued warming. Detection accuracy was high, with an F1 score of 0.87 on the validation set, confirming the robustness of the approach.

expectations: The results paragraph keeps 18,412, 64%, 31% and F1 0.87 as observations
The results paragraph contains no explanation or judgement
The interpretations (coarse resolution, evaporation and drainage, vulnerability, robustness) are listed separately

tasks.prompt: write an abstract from these notes, 200 words max
tasks.audience: Readers of an urban climate journal.
facts: City: Manchester, UK. Period: summer 2022.
Land surface temperature came from Landsat 8 and 9 thermal bands, resampled to 30 m.
Tree canopy cover came from 0.5 m aerial imagery classified with a random forest (overall accuracy 0.91).
Unit of analysis: 1,500 census output areas.

Each 10 percentage points of canopy cover was associated with a 0.8 degree C lower mean afternoon surface temperature (95% CI 0.6 to 1.0), after controlling for building density and distance to water.

Land surface temperature is not air temperature.

tasks.prompt: draft the cover letter for the SAM paper to JAG. one page max

facts: Manuscript title: Interactive segmentation of thaw slumps with the Segment Anything Model and outdated labels.
Corresponding author: Yili Yang, Woodwell Climate Research Center. 12 authors.
What it does: uses old outlines of features as prompts for the Segment Anything Model to segment the features in current imagery, with an interactive tool for expert correction.

tasks.prompt: draft the response to R2.3
tasks.audience: Reviewer 2 and the editor.
facts: The reviewer's comment is in comment.md and what we changed is in changes.md.

materials.comment.md: R2.3: The validation tiles appear to be adjacent to the training tiles. Spatial autocorrelation means the reported accuracy is likely optimistic. The authors should use spatially independent validation.
materials.changes.md: We re-ran the evaluation with ecoregion-blocked folds, so no ecoregion appears in both training and validation. F1 fell from 0.71 to 0.64. We added Table S4 with the blocked results and rewrote Section 3.3 to describe the new split. The main conclusion holds: under blocked folds the multi-region model still beats the single-region model (0.64 against 0.49).

expectations: Leads with what was done, not with long thanks
Points to Section 3.3 and Table S4
States the conclusion that still holds, with its numbers

tasks.prompt: reply to this comment. we won't do it, explain why, be polite
tasks.audience: Reviewer 1 and the editor.
facts: The comment is in comment.md.
The paper is about PlanetScope imagery at 3 m.
Many RTS are smaller than 1 ha, so they are only a few Sentinel-2 pixels (10 m) wide.
A test on Sentinel-2 would need new labels drawn at Sentinel-2 resolution, and none exist for our study area.
We agree that working across sensors matters. We added a sentence to Section 5.3 naming it as future work.

materials.comment.md: R1.5: The authors should test their model on Sentinel-2 imagery as well, to show it generalises across sensors.

expectations: Gives the concrete reasons (slump size against 10 m pixels; no labels at that resolution)
States the change made in Section 5.3

tasks.prompt: write the why-now paragraph for the fellowship application, 200 words
tasks.audience: A multidisciplinary panel; not all are remote sensing experts.
facts: The fellowship is a two-year early-career research fellowship.
Project: track how retrogressive thaw slumps grow from year to year across the Arctic, using PlanetScope images from 2017 to 2025.
Why now, 1: near-daily 3 m PlanetScope imagery has covered the whole Arctic since 2017, so there are now more than eight years of history.
Why now, 2: a circumpolar map of 19,068 slumps, released openly in 2026, gives a starting inventory.
Why now, 3: in parts of the Arctic, slumps have become more active over recent warmer and wetter summers, yet growth rates have been measured at only a few sites.
Growth rates matter for estimating carbon release and for judging risk to roads and buildings.
expectations: Explains concretely why now (the image archive and the inventory)
Explains or avoids specialist terms for a mixed panel

tasks.prompt: write the aims section, 3 aims, 250 words max
tasks.audience: A multidisciplinary review panel.
facts: Project: track how retrogressive thaw slumps grow from year to year across the Arctic, using PlanetScope images from 2017 to 2025, starting from a 2026 inventory of 19,068 slumps.
Aim 1: build a method that links the same slump across years by matching its outlines.
Aim 2: measure growth rates, with uncertainty, for every slump in the inventory over 2017 to 2025.
Aim 3: test which terrain and climate variables explain growth: slope, ground ice content, summer temperature and rainfall.
Outputs: an open dataset of annual growth, open code and a paper.
expectations: Each aim says what will be done and what it delivers
Claims no more than the facts support

tasks.prompt: write my review of this paper. main points only, the editor wants it short
tasks.audience: The editor and the authors.
facts: My notes on the manuscript are in manuscript_notes.md.

materials.manuscript_notes.md:
Manuscript: a new deep learning model that maps landslides from Sentinel-2 imagery, with a reported F1 of 0.93.

Problems:
1. Training and test tiles were split at random from the same three valleys, so spatial autocorrelation probably inflates the scores.
2. Half of the test tiles contain landslides, but landslides cover less than 1% of the region. Precision in real use will be much lower.
3. No comparison with a simple baseline, such as a threshold on NDVI change.
4. The claim that the model generalises globally is not tested; all data come from one country.

Strengths: clearly written, code is shared, and the labelled dataset is useful to others.

My recommendation: major revision.

expectations: Opens with a short summary of what the paper does
Each of the four problems comes with why it matters and what to do

tasks.prompt: project description for my website, the ARTS dataset. 120 words
tasks.audience: Visitors to Yili's personal website: researchers and possible employers.
facts: ARTS (Arctic Retrogressive Thaw Slumps) combines 20 separate thaw slump datasets into one.

tasks.prompt: write the website blurb for the circumpolar slump map. plain language, 150 words
tasks.audience: General visitors to the website, not specialists.
facts: Retrogressive thaw slumps are landslide-like features that form when ice-rich frozen ground thaws on a slope.
A deep learning model scanned 41.5 million tiles of 2025 PlanetScope satellite imagery across the Arctic, run on Google Cloud.
The result: 19,068 quality-checked slump outlines covering 529.7 square km.
Released openly at the NSF Arctic Data Center (doi:10.18739/A26970107) as map layers anyone can download.
Uses: a baseline for tracking change, finding new slumps, planning field work and estimating carbon impacts.
expectations: Explains what a thaw slump is in plain words

tasks.prompt: one paragraph for the research statement on what I work on and why, 200 words
tasks.audience: A hiring committee.
facts: Aim: measure how the Arctic land surface is changing as permafrost thaws, across the whole Arctic, using satellite imagery and deep learning.
Approach: build open labelled datasets (ARTS), models that work at continental scale with few labels, and tests that match real use (rare targets, regions held out from training).
Results so far: a circumpolar thaw slump map (2026); a labelling workflow with the Segment Anything Model that halves the time of manual digitising.
Next: measure how slumps change over time (growth rates) and extend the approach to other rare landforms.
Why it matters: thaw features release carbon and damage infrastructure, but their extent and change are poorly measured.
expectations: The first sentence states the research aim
Gives concrete past results and next steps
